domain: Technology Governance / Legal Theory / Regulatory Design
topic_summary: Analysis of emerging AI regulatory frameworks examining the contested kernel of liability attribution: whether algorithmic harm accountability should rest primarily with developers (who create the systems) or deployers/users (who apply them in specific contexts). This kernel choice restructures the victim/beneficiary topology of algorithmic opacity as a constraint.

key_entities: AI/ML developers (foundation model creators, algorithm designers)
Deployers (organizations implementing AI systems in operational contexts)
End users (individuals subject to algorithmic decisions)
Regulatory authorities (EU AI Act, proposed US frameworks, sectoral regulators)
Opacity as structural property (inscrutability of model internals and training corpus)
Liability as enforcement mechanism (tort law, regulatory penalties, insurance markets)
key_tensions: Generality of capability vs specificity of harm (foundation models vs deployed applications)
Ex ante control authority vs ex post harm realization (who can prevent vs who experiences)
Inscrutability location (model weights vs deployment configuration vs interaction context)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: Liability attribution for algorithmic harm — the foundational question of which party bears legal/financial responsibility when AI systems cause injury
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Legislative and judicial authority to define liable parties; grounded in tort tradition and statutory interpretation

readings.commitment: Developers bear primary liability as creators of the underlying capability
readings.authority_grounding: Product liability doctrine extended to software; strict liability for defective products
readings.expected_structural_delta: Developers enter victim set under regulatory/tort pressure; deployers become beneficiaries of externalized risk; opacity becomes developer's burden to manage or disclose

readings.commitment: Deployers bear primary liability as parties with deployment context control and decision authority
readings.authority_grounding: Agency doctrine and operational control; deployer chooses application domain and can monitor outcomes
readings.expected_structural_delta: Deployers enter victim set; developers externalize deployment risk; opacity becomes deployer's due diligence burden; foundation model providers shielded from downstream harm

readings.commitment: Joint liability distributed along value chain based on causal contribution and control
readings.authority_grounding: Comparative negligence and joint tortfeasor doctrine; multiple party liability apportionment
readings.expected_structural_delta: Both developers and deployers in victim set; coordination costs increase; insurance/indemnification markets emerge; opacity burden distributed via contractual allocation

axiom_contradictions.basis: Developer liability grounds accountability in artifact creation (control precedes deployment); deployer liability grounds it in operational authority (control at harm point). No single framework simultaneously holds that primary accountability rests with the party who lacks control at harm point AND with the party who has it.

axes.human_readable: Developer Liability Reading (Artifact Creator as Primary Responsible Party)
axes.structural_delta: Liability kernel read as: developers bear primary responsibility because they create the capability and control model architecture/training
axes.primary_observable: Regulatory text allocation of liability (EU AI Act provider obligations, US proposed developer requirements); tort case law applying product liability to AI
axes.beneficiary: deployers (risk externalized to developers); end users (recourse against well-capitalized developers)
axes.victim: developers (regulatory compliance costs, litigation risk, insurance burden)
axes.selection_reason: First kernel reading; highest structural impact on regulatory design; reshapes entire accountability topology

axes.human_readable: Deployer Liability Reading (Operational Controller as Primary Responsible Party)
axes.structural_delta: Liability kernel read as: deployers bear primary responsibility because they control deployment context, application choice, and monitoring
axes.primary_observable: Regulatory frameworks emphasizing deployer due diligence (financial services AI use rules, employment discrimination liability for HR algorithms); case law holding operators liable
axes.beneficiary: developers (foundation model providers shielded from downstream liability); innovation velocity (developers face lower risk barrier)
axes.victim: deployers (especially under-resourced organizations lacking AI expertise); end users (if deployers cannot bear costs)
axes.selection_reason: Second kernel reading; structurally opposite to developer reading; same kernel domain but different constraint instantiation

axes.structural_delta: Liability kernel read as: joint responsibility distributed via causal contribution and control tests
axes.primary_observable: Frameworks with split obligations (EU AI Act provider/deployer dual requirements); comparative fault insurance structures
axes.beneficiary: insurance industry (new market for AI liability products); legal profession (litigation complexity)
axes.victim: both developers and deployers (coordination costs, contractual negotiation burden); small actors (cannot afford complex indemnification)
axes.selection_reason: Third kernel reading; captures hybrid/compromise position; demonstrates kernel contestation structure

axes.structural_delta: Model inscrutability as physical constraint of high-dimensional systems
axes.primary_observable: Mechanistic interpretability research failure rates; provable limits on explanation (computational complexity classes)
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: upstream constraint feeding all readings but not itself a kernel reading; true mountain status uncertain (may be piton of research investment choices)

axes.human_readable: End User Legal Standing (Access to Remedy)
axes.structural_delta: Whether harmed individuals can bring claims vs must rely on regulatory enforcement
axes.primary_observable: Private right of action provisions in AI legislation; standing requirements in algorithmic discrimination cases
axes.beneficiary: regulated entities (if standing denied, enforcement limited to under-resourced agencies)
axes.victim: end users (especially marginalized groups facing algorithmic discrimination)
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: downstream of liability kernel; critical for enforcement but structurally dependent on which kernel reading prevails

axes.structural_delta: Whether actuarial risk assessment for algorithmic harm is feasible and at what cost
axes.primary_observable: AI insurance product availability, premium structures, coverage gaps
axes.beneficiary: insurance industry; well-capitalized developers/deployers who can afford coverage
axes.victim: small organizations priced out of compliance; innovation (if insurance unavailable)
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: scaffold dependent on liability regime crystallization; speculative market structure

deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Upstream to all readings but not itself a kernel reading; structural role as constraint substrate rather than liability interpretation; mountain status itself contested (omega_opacity_nature)

deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Downstream of liability kernel; enforcement mechanism dependent on which kernel reading becomes statutory; high-epsilon snare but structurally subordinate to readings

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Whether actuarial risk assessment for algorithmic harm is feasible
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Scaffold dependent on regime crystallization; speculative market dynamics; captured in omega_insurance_availability

omegas.description: Is algorithmic opacity a true Mountain (irreducible inscrutability) or a Piton (research investment choice)? If mechanistic interpretability succeeds, opacity shifts from physical constraint to policy choice, potentially reclassifying all liability readings.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory) + deferred axis opacity_as_mountain

omegas.description: If developer_liability prevails, do foundation model providers withdraw general-purpose API access to avoid liability exposure? If deployer_liability prevails, do under-resourced organizations (nonprofits, municipalities, small businesses) abandon AI adoption? Both readings may suppress deployment in opposite directions.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) + victim structure analysis

omegas.description: Does AI liability insurance market emerge at all? If actuarial assessment fails (harm distributions unknown, adversarial examples undermine risk modeling), insurance unavailability could make ANY liability regime unworkable. Deferred axis insurance_market_emergence becomes structural gate.
omegas.source: Deferred axis insurance_market_emergence + F03 mountain validity concern

omegas.description: Do different jurisdictions crystallize different kernel readings (EU developer-weighted, US deployer-weighted, China state-liability)? If so, global AI deployment faces reading-incompatibility: same harm, multiple liability structures, race-to-bottom forum shopping.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 1 (Operational Medium) — protocol assumes single jurisdiction; cross-border deployment may fracture kernel itself

omegas.description: If end_user_standing is denied (deferred axis), does liability regime become unenforceable? Regulatory agencies lack resources for algorithmic harm monitoring at scale. Private enforcement may be structural necessity regardless of kernel reading.
omegas.source: Deferred high-epsilon axis end_user_standing + enforcement mechanism gap
